fanoutqa_027086.x:
Alcohol and cancer :: Risk factor for specific cancers :: Moderate consumption :: chunk_0010
A 2022 study from the [Seoul National University Hospital](/wiki/Seoul_National_University_Hospital "Seoul National University Hospital"),
over more than 4.5 million of people, who were screened over 7 years,
found that[[45]](#cite_note-seoul_2022-45)

* those who increased alcohol consumption had a higher cancer risk (including, but not limited to, alcohol-related cancers) than those who kept the same level of alcohol intake;
* non-drinkers who became mild drinkers had a risk increase estimated at between 0 and 6 percent (meaning slightly greater risk, not 6 percent risk), while non-drinkers who became "moderate" drinkers had a risk increase estimated between 2 and 18 percent.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

The study also had some limitations. For example, the participants were all registered at the South Korean [National Health Insurance Service](/wiki/Healthcare_in_South_Korea "Healthcare in South Korea"), but the study did not take into account alcohol metabolism diseases which are commonly found in East Asia.[[45]](#cite_note-seoul_2022-45)
The participants were not younger than 40.[[45]](#cite_note-seoul_2022-45)
No data was available to account for positive lifestyle and behaviors held during the screening, that may have influenced the cancer risk, nor for the participants' drinking habits that preceded the screening.[[45]](#cite_note-seoul_2022-45)

A prior study found that, "Increasing but moderate alcohol consumption in women was determined to be associated with an increased risk of cancers of the oral cavity and pharynx, esophagus, larynx, rectum, breast, and liver…".[[47]](#cite_note-pmid19244173-47)

It was released worldwide on July 3, 1996, by [20th Century Fox](/wiki/20th_Century_Fox "20th Century Fox"), but began showing on July 2 (the same day the film's story begins) in original release as a result of a high level of anticipation among moviegoers. The film received mixed to positive reviews, with praise for the performances, musical score and visual effects, but criticism for its characters. It grossed over $817.4 million worldwide,[[2]](#cite_note-BOM-2) becoming the [highest-grossing film of 1996](/wiki/1996_in_film "1996 in film") and the [second-highest-grossing film ever at the time](/wiki/List_of_highest-grossing_films "List of highest-grossing films"), behind *[Jurassic Park](/wiki/Jurassic_Park_(film) "Jurassic Park (film)")* (1993). The film won the [Academy Award for Best Visual Effects](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Visual_Effects "Academy Award for Best Visual Effects") and was nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Sound](/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Sound_Mixing "Academy Award for Best Sound Mixing").[[4]](#cite_note-OscarNight-4)

The sequel, *[Independence Day: Resurgence](/wiki/Independence_Day:_Resurgence "Independence Day: Resurgence")*, was released 20 years later on June 24, 2016, as part of [a planned series of films](/wiki/Independence_Day_(franchise) "Independence Day (franchise)").

The Henley Passport index ranks passports according to the number of destinations that can be reached using a particular country's ordinary passport without the need of a prior visa ("visa-free").[[13]](#cite_note-index_countries-13)[[14]](#cite_note-iata_data-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) The survey ranks 199 passports against 227 destination[[16]](#cite_note-tertiary_2-16) [countries](/wiki/Country "Country"), [territories](/wiki/Territory "Territory"), and [micro-states](/wiki/Microstate "Microstate").[[17]](#cite_note-227_destination-17)[[18]](#cite_note-227_total-18)[[19]](#cite_note-secondary_entrepreneur-19)

Epicentre and associated aftershocks

The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake was unusually large in geographical and geological extent. An estimated 1,600 km (1,000 mi) of [fault surface](/wiki/Fault_(geology) "Fault (geology)") slipped (or ruptured) about 15 m (50 ft) along the [subduction](/wiki/Subduction "Subduction") zone where the [Indian plate](/wiki/Indian_plate "Indian plate") slides under (or subducts) the overriding Burma plate. The slip did not happen instantaneously but took place in two phases over several minutes: Seismographic and acoustic data indicate that the first phase involved a rupture about 400 km (250 mi) long and 100 km (60 mi) wide, 30 km (19 mi) beneath the sea bed—the largest rupture ever known to have been caused by an earthquake. The rupture proceeded at about 2.8 km/s (1.74 mi/s; 10,100 km/h; 6,260 mph), beginning off the coast of [Aceh](/wiki/Aceh "Aceh") and proceeding north-westerly over about 100 seconds. After a pause of about another 100 seconds, the rupture continued northwards towards the [Andaman](/wiki/Andaman_Islands "Andaman Islands") and [Nicobar Islands](/wiki/Nicobar_Islands "Nicobar Islands"). The northern rupture occurred more slowly than in the south, at about 2.1 km/s (1.3 mi/s; 7,600 km/h; 4,700 mph), continuing north for another five minutes to a plate boundary where the fault type changes from subduction to [strike-slip](/wiki/Strike-slip_fault "Strike-slip fault") (the two plates slide past one another in opposite directions).
